analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In אֲנִי יַהְוֶה, “I am Yahweh,” the pronoun is the subject and the divine name identifies the speaker. The following אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ, “who brought you out,” identifies him further by his action.
analysis.morphology: Independent first-person common singular personal pronoun, with no prefix or suffix.
Proper noun, masculine singular, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause describing יַהְוֶה. In אֲנִי יַהְוֶה אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ, “I am Yahweh, who brought you out,” the first-person verb identifies Yahweh as the speaker who brought Abram out.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew relative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אֲנִי יַהְוֶה identifies YHWH as the speaker. The suffix ךָ refers to Abram, and מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים names Ur of the Chaldeans as the place from which YHWH brought him out.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil perfect, first person common singular, with a second person masculine singular object suffix.

analysis.evidence: After הוֹצֵאתִיךָ (“I brought you out”), מֵאוּר names the place of departure. The following כַּשְׂדִּים identifies it as Ur of the Chaldeans.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מִן takes the form מֵ before א. It governs the proper noun אוּר.

analysis.evidence: לְךָ identifies Abram as the recipient, אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת identifies “this land” as the gift, and לְרִשְׁתָּהּ specifies that Abram is to possess it.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לָ־ introduces the Qal infinitive construct תֶת and expresses the purpose of הוֹצֵאתִיךָ (“I brought you out”).
analysis.sense: give land to someone as a possession

analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת means “this land.” It is the territory YHWH promises to give Abram, and the feminine singular suffix in לְרִשְׁתָּהּ refers back to it as the land he is to possess.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ־ prefixes a common noun in the singular absolute. The noun is tagged for both genders and takes feminine singular agreement here with הַזֹּאת.
